item.title: Weekly Learning Report: Dimensionality Reduction & Matrix Factorization
item.dc:creator: Uhjin Kim
item.description:
1 1. Overview

This report explores the mathematical foundations and geometric interpretations of Dimensionality Reduction and Matrix Factorization. We integrate two perspectives:

  1. Geometric Intuition: Understanding operations as rotations, stretchings, and projections.
  2. Algebraic Rigor: Deriving solutions using Eigendecomposition and Optimization techniques.

Our focus is on the two pillars of linear algebra in Data Science: PCA (Principal Component Analysis) and SVD (Singular Value Decomposition).

2 2. Eigendecomposition: The Mathematical Foundation

Before diving into PCA, we must understand the engine that powers it: Eigendecomposition.

2.1 2.1 Concept and Definition

Consider a square matrix . Most vectors change direction when multiplied by . However, there are special vectors that do not change direction, but only scale in length.

An eigenvalue–eigenvector pair satisfies:

  • Eigenvector (): The invariant direction or “axis” of the transformation.
  • Eigenvalue (): The scaling factor along that axis.

If has linearly independent eigenvectors, we can decompose it as:

where is the matrix of eigenvectors and is the diagonal matrix of eigenvalues.

2.2 2.2 Why is this Useful? (Algebraic Power)

Eigendecomposition transforms complex matrix operations into simple scalar operations on the diagonal elements.

  • Powers of a Matrix (): Instead of multiplying matrices times, we simply power the eigenvalues.

  • Inverse ():

  • Determinant: The determinant is the product of all eigenvalues (representing the total volume scaling factor).

2.3 2.3 The Special Case: Symmetric Matrices

For Symmetric Matrices (), such as the Covariance Matrix in PCA, the properties are even stronger (Spectral Theorem):

  1. All eigenvalues are Real.
  2. Eigenvectors corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are Orthogonal.
  3. We can form an Orthonormal Basis .

Note

Interpretation: A symmetric matrix can be viewed as a sum of rank-1 projections. It projects a vector onto an orthogonal axis , scales it by , and sums the results.

2.4 2.4 Decomposing a Vector Using Eigenvectors

A powerful application of eigendecomposition is representing any vector in the coordinate system defined by the eigenvectors. Since the eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix form an orthonormal basis, any vector can be written as:

How do we find the coefficients ? Using the property of orthonormality (), we multiply by :

Thus, the coefficient is simply the projection (inner product) of onto the eigenvector . This is the fundamental principle behind PCA projection.

3 3. PCA (Principal Component Analysis)

PCA projects high-dimensional data onto a lower-dimensional subspace. But how do we choose the best subspace? We have two equivalent interpretations.

3.1 3.1 Geometric Intuition: The Pythagorean Theorem

Consider a data point in 2D space. We want to project it onto a 1D line passing through the origin. For any data point, the relationship between the original vector, its projection, and the error is governed by the Pythagorean Theorem:

  • Hypotenuse (): The inherent energy of the data point. This is Fixed.
  • Base (): The Variance retained (Information).
  • Height (): The Reconstruction Error (Loss).

Since is constant:

3.2 3.2 Mathematical Derivation: Optimization

Let’s prove this mathematically. We seek a unit direction vector () that maximizes the variance of the projected data .

Step 1: Define Objective Given centered data , the covariance matrix is . The variance along direction is:

Step 2: Define Constraint The vector must have unit length:

Step 3: Lagrange Multipliers Construct the Lagrangian function :

Step 4: Solve Take the derivative w.r.t and set to 0:

TipKey Conclusion

The direction that maximizes variance is exactly the Eigenvector of the Covariance Matrix . The variance value itself is the corresponding Eigenvalue .

3.3 3.3 The Algorithm

  1. Center the data: Subtract the mean from each column.
  2. Compute Covariance Matrix: .
  3. Eigen-decomposition: Find eigenvalues and eigenvectors of .
  4. Sort & Select: Sort and pick the top eigenvectors.
  5. Project: .

4 4. SVD (Singular Value Decomposition)

While Eigendecomposition is limited to square matrices, SVD is the fundamental factorization for any rectangular matrix .

4.1 4.1 Geometric Essence: “Circles become Ellipses”

A linear transformation deforms space. If we transform a unit circle (or hypersphere), it is stretched and rotated into a hyper-ellipse. SVD decomposes this transformation into three simple, intuitive steps:

Component Matrix Type Geometric Action
Orthogonal Matrix Rotation: Aligns the input basis to the principal axes of the transformation.
Diagonal Matrix Stretching: Scales the axes by singular values .
Orthogonal Matrix Rotation: Rotates the stretched ellipse to its final orientation in the output space.

4.2 4.2 Computational Strategy: The Trick

Direct calculation of SVD is often done via its relationship to Eigendecomposition.

  • Right Singular Vectors (): These are the eigenvectors of the symmetric matrix . Note: Columns of correspond to the axes in the input space.

  • Left Singular Vectors (): These are the eigenvectors of the symmetric matrix . Note: Columns of correspond to the axes in the output space.

  • Singular Values (): These are the square roots of the eigenvalues of .

4.3 4.3 SVD vs. Eigendecomposition

Feature Eigendecomposition () SVD ()
Scope Square matrices only. Any matrix ().
Basis Input/Output basis are the same (). Input () and Output () bases can differ.
Relationship Finds axes that don’t rotate. Finds axes that map orthogonally to orthogonally.

4.4 4.4 Detailed Geometric Connection

From the eigendecomposition of :

  1. The Eigenvectors of give us the directions in the input space that become the principal axes of the ellipse after transformation.
  2. The Eigenvalues of represent the squared lengths of those axes.

Thus, SVD effectively sorts the “strength” of the transformation along different orthogonal directions.

4.5 4.5 Application: Low-Rank Approximation

SVD allows us to express a matrix as a sum of rank-1 matrices (images):

By keeping only the first largest singular values (truncating the sum), we obtain the optimal rank- approximation of the original matrix. This is the mathematical basis for:

  • Image Compression: Storing only top components.
  • Denoising: Removing small (noise) to reveal the signal.
  • Recommender Systems: Latent Semantic Analysis.

item.title: Weekly Learning Report: Probabilistic Classifiers & Optimization
item.dc:creator: Uhjin Kim
item.description:
1 1. Overview

The core focus of this week’s learning is understanding the mathematical foundations of Probabilistic Classification. Moving beyond simply drawing lines in space to separate data (Geometric Approach), we cover two approaches to modeling the probability that data belongs to a specific class:

  • Discriminative Model (Logistic Regression): Directly models the probability of class given input . The key process is mapping the result of a linear combination to a probability range.
  • Generative Model (Naive Bayes): Models the distribution of data per class and the prior probability , then infers the class inversely using Bayes’ Theorem.

This report integrates the derivation of Logistic Regression based on Odds, Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) for training, and the mathematical proofs and intuition behind the independence assumption in Naive Bayes.

2 2. Logistic Regression: The Discriminative Approach

Logistic Regression is a regression model designed to predict the probability of an event occurrence when the dependent variable is Categorical.

2.1 2.1 The Limits of Linear Regression (Range Mismatch)

Suppose we predict an event using a matrix of vectors and a weight vector . The standard linear regression formula (Linear Combination) is:

Here, a fatal Range Mismatch occurs:

  • LHS (Probability): The probability we want to know, , has a range of .
  • RHS (Linear Eq): The result of has a range of .

Therefore, a linear equation cannot be used directly as a probability; we need a mediator to bridge this gap.

2.2 2.2 Derivation from Odds (From Odds to Logit)

To resolve this mismatch, we introduce the concept of Odds and derive the model in steps.

Step 1: Odds Convert probability into the “ratio of success probability to failure probability.” As probability increases from to , Odds expand from to .

Step 2: Logit (Log-Odds) By taking the natural logarithm of Odds, the range expands to , matching the range of the linear equation . This is called the Logit Transform.

Step 3: Sigmoid Function (Solving for Probability) Rearranging the equation above for , we obtain the activation function (Sigmoid) that converts the linear combination result into a probability.

[Image of sigmoid function curve]

Note

Insight: Logistic regression never abandoned linearity. It combines the simplicity of linear models with the flexibility of probabilistic models through the assumption that “the Log-Odds of the probability are linear.”

2.3 2.3 Multinomial Logistic Regression (Multi-class Extension)

When the result is one of classes, we must extend binary classification. The core idea is **“Setting the last class** as the Pivot.”

For each class , we model the log-odds relative to the pivot class linearly.

Using the constraint that the sum of all probabilities must be 1 (), we can find the denominator (Normalization term).

Rearranging this, the probability of the pivot class is:

The probability for the remaining classes is (Softmax form):

3 3. Optimization: MLE & Loss Function

Now that the model form () is defined, we must find the optimal parameters (i.e., ). We examine how Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) connects to the Loss Function.

3.1 3.1 Likelihood Function

Given observed data , the Likelihood is the joint probability of observing this data viewed as a function of the parameter . Assuming independent and identically distributed (i.i.d) data, it is expressed as a product.

3.2 3.2 Log-Likelihood

As data increases, the product of probabilities tends to zero (Underflow) and is complex to differentiate. Therefore, we take the logarithm to convert the product into a sum. Since the log function is monotonically increasing, the location of the maximum does not change.

To find the optimal solution, we find the point where the partial derivative is 0.

3.3 3.3 From MLE to Loss Function (Equivalence of Minimizing Loss and MLE)

In machine learning, we typically solve “Loss Minimization” problems rather than “Maximization” problems. Consider a binary classification (Bernoulli distribution) scenario. With actual value and predicted value , the likelihood function is:

Taking the negative logarithm () of this yields the familiar Binary Cross-Entropy Loss.

Viewed as a loss function for an individual data point:

TipConclusion

“Maximizing Likelihood” is mathematically identical to “Minimizing the information difference (Cross-Entropy) between the data and the model.”

4 4. Naive Bayes Classifier: The Generative Approach

Naive Bayes views input data as a vector and selects the class with the highest probability using Bayes’ Theorem.

4.1 4.1 Bayes Theorem & Decision Rule

We want to find the Posterior probability .

Here, the denominator, Evidence , is a constant regardless of which class is selected, so it can be ignored (it does not affect the comparison of conditional probabilities).

4.2 4.2 The “Naive” Independence Assumption

The problem lies in computing the likelihood . As features increase, estimating the joint probability distribution becomes nearly impossible. Here, we introduce a powerful and simple (“Naive”) assumption: **“All features** are independent given class .”

4.3 4.3 Final Model and Insight

Finally, the Naive Bayes classifier predicts the class using the following equation:

TipApplication

This is widely used in text classification (e.g., spam filtering). Even though the independence assumption (e.g., “words appear independently”) is rarely true in reality, Naive Bayes often performs surprisingly well because we only need the correct rank of probabilities, not their exact values.

item.title: Weekly Learning Report: MCDM & Similarity Measures
item.dc:creator: Uhjin Kim
item.description:
1 1. Overview

This report explores the mathematical foundations of MCDM and Similarity Measures, focusing on their application in quantative decision-making and high-dimensional data analysis.

2 2. Multi-Criteria Decision Making (MCDM)

2.1 2.1 AHP (Analytic Hierarchy Process)

AHP decomposes a problem into a Hierarchical Structure and uses pairwise comparisons to derive priorities.

  • Step 1: Construct Pairwise Comparison Matrix () For criteria, construct a matrix where represents the relative importance of element over element . (Property: )

  • Step 2: Calculate Priority Vector () Mathematically, this involves solving the eigenvalue problem: In practice (Synthesization method):

    1. Normalize each column of :
    2. Average the rows to find weights:

  • Step 3: Consistency Verification To ensure the decision maker’s logic is consistent:

    1. Calculate Consistency Index (CI):
    2. Calculate Consistency Ratio (CR): (Where is the Random Index based on matrix size . If , consistency is acceptable.)
TipInsight: Handling Subjectivity

The core strength of AHP lies in the Consistency Ratio (CR). Unlike simple weighted scoring, AHP mathematically quantifies ‘how inconsistent the decision maker is.’ If , it forces the decision maker to re-evaluate their logic, ensuring rational consistency in subjective judgments.

2.2 2.2 ANP (Analytic Network Process)

ANP generalizes AHP by overcoming the assumption of independence among criteria, handling interdependence using a supermatrix approach.

  • Step 1: Construct Unweighted Supermatrix Perform pairwise comparisons (like AHP) for all interacting clusters and nodes. Place the resulting local priority vectors into a block matrix.

  • Step 2: Construct Weighted Supermatrix Since the unweighted matrix is not column-stochastic (columns sum > 1), multiply each block by the priority of its corresponding cluster so that each column sums to 1.

  • Step 3: Calculate Limiting Supermatrix Raise the weighted supermatrix to a large power to capture all indirect influences until the values stabilize (converge). The resulting rows represent the final global priorities of the elements.

NoteWhy ANP matters in Engineering?

Real-world industrial systems are rarely linear hierarchies. For instance, Product Quality affects Sales, but increased Sales might lower Quality due to production pressure (Feedback Loop). ANP captures this interdependence via the Supermatrix, making it superior for complex system modeling.

2.3 2.3 DEMATEL

DEMATEL is specialized for visualizing the Cause & Effect structure of complex factors.

  • Step 1: Direct Relation Matrix () Create an matrix based on expert evaluation (scale 0~4), where is the direct influence of on .

  • Step 2: Normalization () Normalize the matrix so that values fall between 0 and 1.

  • Step 3: Total Relation Matrix () Calculate the sum of direct and all indirect effects using the geometric series formula (where is the identity matrix):

  • Step 4: Causal Parameters

    • Prominence (): (Row sum) + (Col sum). Represents total importance.
    • Relation (): If positive, factor is a Cause; if negative, it is an Effect.

2.4 2.4 TOPSIS

TOPSIS ranks alternatives based on their geometric distance to ideal solutions.

NoteKey Concept
  • PIS (Positive Ideal Solution, ): The hypothetical solution that maximizes benefit and minimizes cost.
  • NIS (Negative Ideal Solution, ): The hypothetical solution that minimizes benefit and maximizes cost.

  • Step 1: Vector Normalization Normalize the decision matrix () to eliminate unit differences.

  • Step 2: Weighted Normalized Matrix () Multiply by the weights () of each criterion.

  • Step 3: Determine Ideal Solutions

    • PIS (): Max value for benefits (), Min value for costs ().
    • NIS (): Min value for benefits (), Max value for costs ().

  • Step 4: Calculate Distances & Closeness

    • Separation from PIS:
    • Separation from NIS:
    • Relative Closeness (): (Rank alternatives by in descending order.)

3 3. Measurement Metrics

These measures provide the mathematical foundation for quantifying relationships between data objects.

3.1 3.1 Similarity Measures

  • Cosine Similarity: Measures the cosine of the angle between two non-zero vectors. It focuses on orientation rather than magnitude. (Range: 0 to 1 for positive vector spaces)

  • Jaccard Index: Measures similarity between finite sample sets.

3.2 3.2 Distance Measures

  • Euclidean Distance: The straight-line distance between two points in Euclidean space ( norm).

  • Manhattan Distance: The distance between two points measured along axes at right angles ( norm).

  • Hellinger Distance: Used to quantify the similarity between two probability distributions.

WarningThe Curse of Dimensionality

In high-dimensional spaces (e.g., text data with 10,000+ features), the relative difference between the nearest and farthest data points becomes negligible. Thus, Euclidean Distance often loses its discriminatory power. In such sparse environments, Cosine Similarity is generally preferred as it focuses on the “direction” rather than the magnitude.

3.3 3.3 Node Centrality (Network Analysis)

Measures the importance of nodes within a graph.

Measure Definition
Degree Centrality The number of direct links connected to a node.
Closeness Centrality The reciprocal of the sum of the shortest path distances from a node to all other nodes.
Betweenness Centrality The extent to which a node lies on the shortest paths between other nodes.
Eigenvector Centrality A measure of influence where connections to high-scoring nodes contribute more to the score.

item.title: pLSA and Review Mining
item.dc:creator: Uhjin Kim
item.description:
This page reviews a paper published by the Business Intelligence and Data Analytics Lab at Konkuk University, Seoul, Korea. This review is written for study and documentation purposes.

Reference:
Jeong Jaeyeon, Jiho Lee and Janghyeok Yoon. (2023). Service Opportunity Discovery Via Review Mining of Meal Kit Delivery Service. Journal of the Korean Institute of Industrial Engineers, 49(2), 142-156.

정재연, 이지호 and 윤장혁. (2023). 밀키트 구독서비스의 리뷰 마이닝을 통한 서비스 기회 발굴. 대한산업공학회지, 49(2), 142-156.

1 1. Research Overview

1.1 Background and Objective

Existing research on meal kit subscription services has been limited to presenting single keywords, which fails to consider the context of consumer feedback. Accordingly, this study aims to discover new product opportunities by utilizing quantitative metrics based on Review Mining.

1.2 Analysis Process

The research proceeds through the following four-step process:

  1. Data Collection & Preprocessing: Crawling review data and extracting keywords.

  2. Topic Modeling (LDA): Identifying service topics and calculating Importance scores.

  3. Sentiment Analysis: Calculating Satisfaction scores through keyword sentiment analysis.

  4. Opportunity Discovery: Constructing a Service Opportunity Map and identifying opportunity areas.

2 2. Detailed Methodology

2.1 A. Data Preprocessing and Keyword Extraction

Using the RAKE algorithm, an initial set of 24,337 keywords was extracted. After removing stopwords (numbers, special characters, etc.) and filtering for adjectives/adverbs, a final set of 2,161 keywords related to subscriptions was selected.

2.2 B. Topic Identification (Topic Modeling)

The LDA (Latent Dirichlet Allocation) algorithm was used to identify topics. To determine the optimal number of topics (), the Elbow Method was employed. This method selects the point where cosine similarity decreases (indicating higher independence) as the number of topics increases.

Code 
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

k = list(range(1, 11))
distortion = [1300, 1000, 800, 700, 650, 600, 580, 550, 520, 500]

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
plt.plot(k, distortion, marker='o', linestyle='-', color='blue')
plt.title('Elbow Method')
plt.xlabel('Number of clusters')
plt.ylabel('Distortion')
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()

2.3 C. Metric Calculation: Importance & Satisfaction

This study quantifies “Importance” and “Satisfaction” using the probability distributions derived from Topic Modeling and Sentiment Analysis.

2.3.1 1. Importance Score

Importance determines how heavily a topic is discussed by customers. It is calculated by summing the topic contribution probabilities () across all documents in the Document-Topic Matrix.

  • Logic: A topic mentioned frequently across many reviews is considered a critical service element.

  • Normalization: The raw sum is normalized to a scale of 0 to 10 using Min-Max Normalization.

2.3.2 2. Satisfaction Score

Satisfaction reflects the customer’s sentiment toward a specific topic. It is calculated by integrating sentiment analysis with the Topic-Keyword Matrix ().

  • Step 1: Keyword Sentiment ()
    Since the same word can have different meanings depending on context, the sentiment score of a keyword is defined as the average sentiment score of all sentences containing that keyword. (where is the set of sentences containing word )

  • Step 2: Topic Satisfaction ()
    The satisfaction of a topic is the weighted sum of the sentiment scores of its keywords, weighted by the keyword’s probability within that topic.

  • Normalization: Like importance, the final satisfaction score is normalized to a scale of 0 to 10.

2.4 D. Service Opportunity Map

Service topics are diagnosed by plotting them on axes of Importance and Satisfaction.

  • Under-served: Areas with high Importance but low Satisfaction. These represent key improvement opportunities.
  • Over-served: Areas with low Importance but excessively high Satisfaction.
  • Right-served: Areas where Importance and Satisfaction are balanced.

Opportunity Score Algorithm:

The size of the circle in the map is proportionate to the Opportunity Score.

3 3. Theoretical Background: pLSA

3.1 pLSA (Probabilistic Latent Semantic Analysis)

pLSA is a latent variable model that associates unobserved class variables (topics, ) with observed data (documents and words ). The joint probability model (Symmetric formulation) is defined as:

To estimate the parameters , we aim to maximize the Likelihood of the observed data.

3.2 1. Likelihood Function ()

Assuming the data is independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.), the total likelihood is the product of the probabilities of all observed document-word pairs occurring times:

Substituting the generative model into the likelihood:

3.3 2. Log-Likelihood Function ()

Since maximizing a product is computationally difficult, we maximize the log-likelihood . The logarithm is a monotonic function, so the maximum location remains unchanged.

Problem: The summation exists inside the logarithm. This makes direct maximization via partial derivatives intractable because the parameters are coupled. To solve this, we use the EM Algorithm.

3.4 3. Derivation of the Surrogate Function (Q-Function)

Direct maximization of is difficult due to the summation inside the logarithm. To overcome this, we employ the EM algorithm, which iteratively maximizes a lower bound of the log-likelihood constructed using Jensen’s Inequality.

3.4.1 A. Constructing the Lower Bound

Let be the current parameters and be the parameters from the previous iteration. We introduce the posterior probability of the latent variable , denoted as , which sums to 1 over ().

We can rewrite the log-likelihood by multiplying and dividing by this probability term:

3.4.2 B. Applying Jensen’s Inequality

Since the logarithm function is strictly concave, Jensen’s Inequality states that the log of the expectation is greater than or equal to the expectation of the log ().

Applying this to the equation above:

Here, serves as the Lower Bound for the true log-likelihood.

3.4.3 C. Defining the Q-Function

We expand the Lower Bound:

The second term, , depends only on the old parameters and is constant with respect to . Therefore, maximizing the Lower Bound is equivalent to maximizing the first term, which we define as the Q-function:

In the M-step, we maximize this -function to find the optimal .

3.5 4. EM Algorithm Steps

The EM algorithm alternates between estimating the latent variables (E-step) and optimizing the parameters (M-step) until convergence.

3.5.1 A. E-Step (Expectation): Posterior Probability Estimation

In this step, we assume the current parameters are fixed. We calculate the posterior probability that an observed occurrence of word in document originated from topic . This posterior probability, , serves as a “soft assignment” or weight.

Applying Bayes’ Theorem:

3.5.2 B. M-Step (Maximization): Parameter Update

In this step, we update the parameters to maximize the -function calculated in the E-step. Since these parameters represent probabilities, they must satisfy the normalization constraints (i.e., they must sum to 1).

We solve this constrained optimization problem using Lagrange Multipliers.

1) Updating Topic-Word Distribution * Constraint: * Update Rule:

2) Updating Topic-Document Distribution * Constraint: * Update Rule:

3) Updating Topic Prior * Constraint: * Update Rule:

The E-step and M-step are repeated iteratively until the increase in the log-likelihood falls below a predefined threshold ().

4 4. Practical Implementation: pLSA with Python

To bridge the gap between theory and practice, we implement a topic modeling experiment using a small synthetic corpus. This experiment demonstrates how the model distinguishes between IT, Economy, and Food topics, and how it handles documents with mixed topics.

4.1 A. Environment Setup & Data Preparation

We construct a Term-Document Matrix () from a list of documents. doc_8 (“Python code for stock market analysis”) is intentionally designed to contain keywords from both IT and Economy topics to test the model’s soft-clustering capabilities.

Code

from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer
from sklearn.decomposition import NMF

documents = [
    "Python code is simple and easy",
    "I like python programming language",
    "computer memory and cpu execution",
    "Stock market price is going up",
    "Invest money in the future market",
    "Wall street analyzes the stock price",
    "Apple banana and peach salad",
    "I like to eat apple and banana",
    "Python code for stock market analysis"
]

vectorizer = CountVectorizer(stop_words='english')
dtm = vectorizer.fit_transform(documents)
feature_names = vectorizer.get_feature_names_out()

df_dtm = pd.DataFrame(dtm.toarray(), columns=feature_names, 
                      index=[f"doc_{i}" for i in range(len(documents))])

5 5. Key Takeaways

5.1 Importance of Keyword Filtering

The implementation demonstrates a critical challenge inherent in topic modeling: the resulting topic-keyword matrices frequently contain adjectives and adverbs that lack semantic relevance to the extracted topics. To address this limitation, domain-specific keyword pre-filtering is essential—researchers should manually curate keyword sets prior to topic extraction to ensure topical coherence and interpretability of the final results.
